I've backed a bunch of stuff on Kickstarter, and yeah, delays are pretty common. From video games, I got Mighty No 9 (big disappointment), Yooka Layley (still waiting for the Switch version, but not too keen on it at this point either), and Bloodstained (Still have strong hopes for, but might be the same category). I have probably 10-15 Kickstarters I'm waiting for fulfillment on, and I've been all over the gammut on delays and quality issues.

 

My biggest complaint with OblivAeon was more a complaint with GTG Kickstarter practice in 2016; I backed every game GTG put a Kickstarter up for that year (with the exception of Exoplanets, which I picked up on release since I actually had funds then). From an outside perspective looking in, it felt like they spread themselves too thin by trying to publish too many things at once, and as a result each project added more delay to the others already in flight. I won't say it's unreasonable to have multiple things in flight, but when you have 6+ projects in the air at the same time and they all end up late, that raises a red flag.

(Mind you, I was disatisfied with the delays, but I've been happy with backing every one of those games once I had them in hand and they hit the table. I also admittedly like to gripe, so there's that.)

 

My second issue with the OblivAeon delays is more personal in that, while the OblivAeon fight is cool, he won't be hitting my table as often as the original villains/the occasional game of Vengeance. He feels more like a once every 6 months - a year kind of experience, that you have to be in the mood for, rather than a completely new game mode that will always serve in rotation. He definitely won't be in my go-to list when I want to play a random game of Sentinels. The stuff I really want (the new heroes-- especially Void Guard, Stuntman, and Benchmark), however, have been completed for a while and are just waiting for OblivAeon to be finalized to ship out.

Add to that the months of mangled communication, especially around the delays, and a couple of people who will defend any criticism against GTG as invalid, regardless if the raised criticisms are warranted or not, left a very sour taste in my mouth for the experience.

The goal of Clang was to bring realistic sword-fighting to computer/video games, by developing a system that would allow you complex control (vs. "left click to swing").  It was going to (initially at least) be based around Fiore dei Liberi's work, and at the time I was studying European medieval martial arts so that was very exciting to me.  It was a pretty experimental project, and the "game" it would've delivered would have been geared to demonstrate the system, which then hopefully other games would use.  Unfortunately they used up all the money working on it before finishing, and never found a company willing to try the system out, so they had to close up shop.

I was disappointed that it didn't deliver, but it was also clearly more experimental in nature and I knew that going in, so I my disappointment was mostly that I didn't get complex sword-fighting games.  I certainly didn't feel like I had wasted my money or anything.

I would definitely include those two, although with caveats.

I'm not sure I'd put Mr. Fixer at a 2 anyway, he's a very straightforward character who just has to carefully evaluate which style and tool he wants (when he even has a choice).  If some of the variant 1's deserve to stay 1's, normal Mr. Fixer should be a 1, too.  DW Fixer is a high 2 or a low 3, since he has to make continuous sacrifices to do anything at all, especially in rounds 2-3 or so (or after a wipe).  He's very hard to build up, and has to play a continuous balancing game between damage now and options later.  And he has to have solid awareness of what every other hero is doing to know whether they can spare something to fuel his attack.

Hunted Naturalist should be a 3 for the same reason The Sentinels and Setback are: more stuff to keep track of.  I break out some small tokens or toys to mark what form he's currently emulating, and any time you have to do that I think a 3 is merited.  His strategy isn't any more complex, but his mechanic is.  It's very similar to Sky-Scraper in many ways, who is also a well-deserved 3.

Completionist Guise is also easily a 3.  You have to know what variants are in the box and the best circumstances to switch your whole team between all of them.  Although with all of Guise's bizarre interactions, he may deserve to be a 3 anyway.  Completionist might just be the most complicated hero in the game.

Xtreme Captain Cosmic is pushing it.  He can suicide very, very easily.  Fortunately he does have a couple of alternate powers he can give himself.  But he might again deserve to be a low 2 in his normal form and a high 2 in Xtreme form.

I haven't played with Setting Sun Ra yet, but he reads like a lighter version of DW Mr. Fixer.  He has a much more complex resource management game to play.  He's defninitely not a 3, and he can always put out cards that give him alternate powers, but I don't think he's a 1 either.

Most of the others whose variants are much more complex than their base card–Termi-Nation Unity, BoT Chrono-Ranger, Rogue KNYFE, Xtreme Haka, PW Fanatic, Termi-Nation Bunker, F5 Bunker, F6 Tempest, PW Tempest–do tend to transition to using powers from cards as soon as they can get them, and their powers don't make it any harder to reach that point, so Christopher's logic is good here.  But for heroes that depend heavily on their base power throughout the game, and for whom that power is a core mechanic, I think he's wrong.

You do make an interesting point in that "complexity" is not clearly defined.  For instance, in some cases of 3's (The Sentinels, Nightmist, Setback, Sky-Scraper), it's just a slightly odd mechanic that doesn't appear anywhere else in the game but isn't hard to understand or manage.  In some (AZ, Scholar) it's because they have resource management that don't work the same way as most other heroes (and when did Scholar get bumped up to a 3?) and which sometimes results in multi-step math.  In one (Argent Adept) it's mostly because he easily gets flooded with options and has a lot to consider every round, and plan for future rounds.  It's not consistent and it's often hard to compare.

Tempest was using everything he had to fend off waves of Aeon men within the winding hallways the Court of Blood, when a massive earthquake struck, shaking the ornate walls with such ferocity, that the heroes and vampires stopped fighting. Tempest turned around and saw a Zhu Long warrior let out a bloodcurdling scream, a noise that not even the Countess has heard in her lifetime. The screaming only ceased when he was torn out of existence, every part of him shredded into nothingness. Then there was nothing. The world stopped shaking, and the only noises the inhabitants could hear were the distant footsteps of Aeon men, and the blood dripping from the walls.  The Harpy collapsed to her knees, and shuddered. "They…they… didn't make it." As the footsteps grew louder, the heroes knew they couldn't stop. They needed to save everyone. They needed to save everything.
